newsitem.title: USA: Texas executes Mexican convicted in 1985 murder.
newsitem.headline: Texas executes Mexican convicted in 1985 murder.

text.p: A Mexican whose death sentence angered his countrymen was put to death on Wednesday in the third execution in as many days at the state prison here.

Irineo Tristan Montoya, 30, was strapped to a gurney and injected with a dose of lethal chemicals hours after the U.S. Supreme Court rejected a final appeal arguing that his diplomatic rights had been violated after his arrest.

"Goodbye. I wait for you in heaven. I will be waiting for you. I love my parents. I am at peace with God. Fight for the good," Tristan said. He gasped twice after he was injected with a dose of lethal chemicals and died shortly after 6 p.m. CDT (2300 GMT).

Moments before he died, a holy card tucked under his shirt, Tristan smiled and spoke softly to his father and common-law wife who witnessed the execution along with reporters and prison officials behind a glass partition at the death chamber of the Huntsville State Prison.

Tristan was sentenced to die for the November 1985 murder of John Kilheffer, who was stabbed more than 22 times and his body dumped in a grapefruit grove near the Rio Grande. Arrested two weeks later, Tristan confessed to his involvement in the killing but said another Mexican, Juan Villavicencio, actually killed the American, prosecutors said.

His fate sparked protests on both sides of the border. In Mexico, protesters gathered for the past two days on a bridge between Matamoros and Brownsville, Texas, calling on Texas to halt the execution.

Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria sent a letter on Wednesday to Texas Gov. George Bush urging him to stay the execution on humanitarian grounds for 30 days while a final investigation into the case was carried out.

But the U.S. Supreme Court late on Wednesday rejected Tristan's last-minute appeal, and Bush, who cannot grant clemency under state law, refused a request to delay the execution to allow the courts more time to consider further appeals.

One of 12 Mexicans on the Texas death row, Tristan's death sentence stirred deep passions in his home country where there is no death penalty. But the case drew scant attention in Texas, a state founded on frontier justice that has executed a record 24 people this year.
"This is no different than any other execution, not as far as we are concerned," prison spokesman David Nunnelee said.

Texas leads the nation in the number of executions since the Supreme Court reinstated the death penalty in 1976 and the rapid pace this year has sparked renewed protests from international human rights groups.
Tristan's execution was witnessed by his father and two brothers, but Mexico consul-general Manuel Perez Cardenas declined an invitation at the last minute.

"The government decided that my presence wouldn't be helpful in any sense because Mexico is absolutely clear in its position against this punishment," he said, adding the execution would not strain ties between Mexico and its northern neighbours.

A shrimper who spent 11 years on death row, Tristan earlier in the day bid goodbye to his family, remaining calm even as protesters gathered outside the prison to begin a vigil in the hours before he was set to die.
"Why did they wait 11 years only to take away my son from me," his mother, Emilia Montoya, who suffers from cancer, said as she joined a group of protesters outside the prison.

Tristan spent his last day on death row visiting with relatives and his lawyer. He turned down a chance to walk in the prison yard, and ordered a final meal of fish, french fries, jalapenos, carrots and ice cream.
